Surah "al-'Alaq" (The Clot). It is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma'), and according to the statement of Abu Musa and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed. It has nineteen verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ (1)

This surah is the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed, according to the view of most commentators (mufassirun). Jibril (Gabriel) came with it to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was standing on Hira', and he taught him five verses from this surah. It has also been said that the first revelation was ﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:1). This was stated by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and it has already been discussed [[See vol. 19, p. 58 of the first edition and vol. 19, p. 59 of the second edition.]]. It has also been said that the first revelation was the Opening Surah (al-Fatihah), as stated by Abu Maysara al-Hamdani. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the first thing revealed of the Qur'an was ﴿Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ (al-An'am 6:151) [[Verse 151 of Surat al-An'am.]]. The correct view, however, is the first one. 'A'isha said: the beginning of what was granted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of revelation was true dreams (al-ru'ya al-sadiqah) [[So it is in the originals and in Muslim. In al-Bukhari it reads: "al-salihah" (the good dreams).]], and the angel came to him and said: "Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous." This was narrated by al-Bukhari. In the two Sahihs, also from her, she said: The beginning of the revelation granted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was true dreams in sleep. He would not see a dream except that it came like the break of dawn. Then seclusion became beloved to him, so he would seclude himself in the cave of Hira', devoting himself to worship (yatahannath) [[Yatahannath means he worships, from the verb "tahannuth". It is said: "So-and-so yatahannath," meaning he does an act by which he removes himself from sin and distress.]] there for many nights, [before returning to his family [[An addition from the two Sahihs.]]] and taking provisions for that. Then he would return to Khadijah and take provisions for the like of it, until the Truth came upon him while he was in the cave of Hira'. The angel came to him and said: [Read.] He said: "I am not one who reads." He said: "Then he seized me and squeezed me (faghhani) [[al-Ghatt means fierce pressure and compression.]] until I reached the limit of my exertion, then he released me," and said: [Read.] I said: "I am not one who reads." Then he seized me and squeezed me a third time until I reached the limit of my exertion, then he released me and said: [Read in the name of your Lord who created. Created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous. Who taught by the pen. Taught man what he did not know.] [The hadith in full.] Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi said: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari used to come around to us in this mosque, the mosque of Basra, and seat us in circles and teach us the Qur'an. I can still see him between his two white garments, and from him I learned this surah: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾, and it was the first surah that Allah revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ). 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, related that it was the first surah revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), followed after it by ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ (al-Qalam), then after it ﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾, then after it ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ (al-Duha). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Zuhri said: The first thing revealed was the surah ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ up to His words ﴿what he did not know﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grieved, and began to climb the high peaks of the mountains. Jibril came to him and said: "You are the Prophet of Allah." He returned to Khadijah and said: [Wrap me up, and pour cold water over me.] Then ﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾ was revealed (al-Muddaththir 74:1).

The meaning of ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ is: read what has been revealed to you of the Qur'an, beginning with the name of your Lord. This means that you mention the basmala at the beginning of every surah. The position of the particle "bi" (ba') in ﴿bi-smi rabbika﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It has also been said that "bi" has the meaning of "ʿala" (upon), meaning: read upon the name of your Lord. It is said: "He did such-and-such in the name of Allah" and "upon the name of Allah." According to this view, the object of reading is omitted, meaning: read the Qur'an and open it with the name of Allah. Some people said: the name of your Lord is the Qur'an, so the meaning is: "Read by the name of your Lord," that is, "read the name of your Lord," and the "ba'" is extra (za'idah), like the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿grows with oil﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:20), and as the poet said:

"Black-eyed, they do not recite with the surahs" [[This is the second half of a verse by al-Ra'i, whose first half is: "They are free women, not mothers of mares."]]

He meant: they do not recite the surahs. It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ is: mention His name. He was commanded to begin the recitation with the name of Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 96, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Created man﴾, meaning the son of Adam.

(﴿from a clinging substance﴾) i.e., from blood, plural of ʿalaqah (a clot of blood, a clinging substance). The ʿalaqah is congealed blood, and when it flows, it is al-masfuh (poured-forth blood). He said "from ʿalaq," mentioning it in the plural form, because by "al-insan" He intended the collective, and all of them were created from ʿalaq after the nutfah (drop of seminal fluid). The ʿalaqah is a piece of moist blood, named so because, due to its moisture, it clings to whatever it passes over; when it dries, it is no longer an ʿalaqah. The poet said:

"We left him falling upon his hands,
Spitting upon them the clinging blood of the jugular vein."

He singled out man for mention to honor him. It was also said: He intended to show the extent of His blessing upon him, by creating him from a base clot, until he became a complete human being and a rational, discerning person.

Allah the Exalted said: "Recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous" (3).

His saying, "Recite," is emphasis, and the statement is complete. Then He began anew and said: "And your Lord is the Most Generous," meaning, the Generous (al-Karim).

Al-Kalbi said: it means the Forbearing (al-Halim) toward the ignorance of His servants, so He did not hasten their punishment. The first interpretation is more fitting to the meaning, because when He mentioned the blessings He had bestowed earlier, He indicated by them His generosity. It has also been said: "Recite, and your Lord," meaning, recite, O Muhammad, and your Lord will help you and grant you understanding, even though you were not a reader. And "al-Akram" means the one who overlooks the ignorance of His servants.

**First issue:** Al-Qurtubi's commentary on the verse ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾ (96:4).

There are three questions concerning it. The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who taught by the pen﴾, meaning writing and script. That is, He taught man the script by means of the pen. Sa'id reported from Qatadah that he said: "The pen is a great blessing from God, Exalted is He. Without it, religion would not stand and livelihood would not be set right." This points to the completeness of His generosity, glorified is He, in that He taught His servants what they did not know, and moved them from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge. It also draws attention to the excellence of the knowledge of writing, because of the great benefits in it, which none encompasses except Him. The sciences were not recorded, wisdom was not preserved, the reports and sayings of the earlier peoples were not kept, and the revealed books of God were not preserved except through writing. Were it not for writing, the affairs of religion and of this world would not be upright. It is called a *qalam* (pen) because it is *yuqlam*, that is, cut, and from this comes *taqlim al-zufr* (paring of the nails).

Some of the later poets, describing the pen, said:

"It is as though, with the ink dyeing its head,
it is an old man adorning himself for the union with a coy maiden."

"Why should I not regard it with reverence,
and by it the scrolls are raised up to God?"

[Note from the source: In the manuscripts, "*alla*" appears in place of "*lima la*" (why not), which is probably a scribal error.]

It is reported from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "O Messenger of God, shall I write down what I hear from you of ḥadīth?" He said: "Yes, write, for God taught by the pen." Mujahid reported from Abu Umar that he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, created four things with His own hand, then said to the rest of creation, 'Be,' and it was: the pen, the Throne, the Garden of Eden, and Adam, peace be upon him."

As to whom He taught by the pen, there are three opinions. The first is that it is Adam, peace be upon him, because he was the first to write; this was said by Ka'b al-Ahbar. The second is that it is Idris, who was the first to write; this was said by al-Dahhak. The third is that it includes everyone who wrote with the pen, because no one was taught except by God's teaching, Exalted is He. By this He combined His blessing upon man in His creation with His clarifying His blessing upon him in teaching him, to complete the blessing upon him.

The second question: It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ, through the ḥadīth of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When God created the creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him above the Throne: 'Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath.'" It is also firmly established from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "The first thing God created was the pen. He said to it, 'Write.' It wrote what would be until the Day of Resurrection, and it is with Him in the Remembrance above His Throne." In the Sahih, from the ḥadīth of Ibn Mas'ud, that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "When the drop of semen has passed forty-two nights, God sends an angel to it, who shapes it, creates its hearing, its sight, its skin, its flesh and its bones. Then he says, 'O Lord, male or female?' and your Lord decrees what He wills, and the angel writes. Then he says, 'O Lord, its term,' and your Lord says what He wills, and the angel writes. Then he says, 'O Lord, its provision,' so that your Lord may decree what He wills, and the angel writes. Then the angel comes out with the scroll in his hand, and he adds nothing to what he was commanded and omits nothing." And God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing﴾ (82:10–11).

[Note from the source: Verse 10 of Surat al-Infitar.]

Our scholars said: The pens are, in origin, three. The first pen is the one God created with His own hand and commanded to write. The second pen is the pens of the angels, which God placed in their hands, with which they write the decrees, the occurrences and the deeds. The third pen is the pens of people, which God placed in their hands, with which they write their speech and by which they attain their aims. There are many virtues in writing. Writing is part of eloquent expression, and eloquent expression is among what is distinctive to the human being.

The third question: Our scholars said: The Arabs were the least of people in knowledge of the Book, and the least of the Arabs in knowledge of it was the Chosen one ﷺ, who was turned away from knowing it, so that this would be more firmly established as proof of his miracle and stronger as his argument. This has already been explained in detail in Surat al-'Ankabut.

[Note from the source: See vol. 13, p. 351.]

Hammad ibn Salamah reported from al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Salam, from Ayyub ibn Abdullah al-Fihri, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not let your women dwell in upper chambers, and do not teach them writing." Our scholars said: The Prophet ﷺ only warned them of this because letting women dwell in upper chambers leads to their looking out toward men, and there is no protection or concealment for them in that. For they cannot control themselves, so that when they overlook men, temptation and trial arise. So he warned them against making upper chambers for them, as a means to temptation.

It is as the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There is no good for women better than that men should not see them, and they should not see men." This is because she was created from the man, so her desire is for the man, and the man was created with desire, and she was made a dwelling for him. Thus neither of them can be trusted with the other. Likewise, teaching writing may at times be a cause of temptation, for when she is taught writing she writes to the one she desires. Writing is one of the eyes, by which the absent is seen by the present, and script is the traces of a hand. In it is the expression of what is in the heart by means the tongue cannot utter, and it is more eloquent than speech. So the Messenger of God ﷺ loved to cut off from them the causes of temptation, as a protection for them and a purity for their hearts.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 96, verse 5:

It was said: "al-insan" here refers to Adam, peace be upon him. He taught him the names of everything, in accordance with what the Qur'an mentions in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [[Qur'an 2:31.]]. Nothing was left out, for Allah, glorified is He, taught Adam the name of each thing in every language, and Adam mentioned it to the angels just as he had been taught. Through this his virtue became manifest, his worth was made clear, his prophethood was established, and the proof of Allah against the angels and His argument were confirmed. The angels complied with the command, because they saw the nobility of the situation, witnessed the majesty of power, and heard of the great matter. Then his offspring inherited this knowledge, generation after generation, and passed it on from people to people. This has already been discussed in full in surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 279, second edition.]], and all praise is due to Allah.

It was also said: "al-insan" here refers to the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ [[Qur'an 4:113.]] [al-Nisa': 113]. On this view, the meaning of "He taught you" (ʿallamaka) is the future tense, since this was among the first things revealed.

It was also said: it is general, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [[Qur'an 16:78.]] [al-Nahl: 78].

Allah's saying: (Nay! Indeed, man surely transgresses) to the end of the surah. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It was also said: the whole surah was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, when the Prophet ﷺ forbade him from prayer, so Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to pray at the Masjid and to recite "in the name of your Lord." On this view, the surah is not among the first things revealed. It is possible that the first five verses were the first revelation, and then the remainder was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, and the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to join that to the beginning of the surah, because the arrangement of the surahs took place by command of Allah. Do you not see that His saying, Exalted is He: (And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah) [Al-Baqarah: 281] was the last thing revealed, and yet it is joined to what was revealed long before it? (Kalla) means "truly," since nothing precedes it. (Al-insan) here is Abu Jahl. (At-tughyan) is exceeding the limit in disobedience. (An ra'ahu) means "because he saw himself," i.e., he became one who has wealth and property. Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Abu Salih from him, said: when this verse was revealed and the polytheists heard of it, Abu Jahl came to him and said: "O Muhammad, you claim that whoever becomes rich transgresses; so make the mountains of Makkah gold for us, so that perhaps we may take from them, and then we will transgress, abandon our religion, and follow your religion." He said: then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "O Muhammad, give them the choice in that matter: if they wish, We will do to them what they asked; but if they do not believe, We will do to them as We did to the companions of the table (al-Ma'idah)." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that the people would not accept that, so he refrained from them out of mercy toward them. It was also said: (an ra'ahu) means "because he saw himself sufficient through his tribe, his helpers and his supporters." The lam has been omitted from His saying (an ra'ahu), as one says: "Indeed you transgress if you see your wealth." Al-Farra' said: he did not say "ra'a nafsahu" (saw himself), as one says "qatala nafsahu" (killed himself), because ra'a is among the verbs that require a subject and a predicate, like "zann" (think) and "hasiba" (reckon), so it is not limited to one object. The Arabs omit the nafs (self) in this category: they say ra'aytani and hasibtani, and mata tarakа kharijan, and mata tazunnuka kharijan. Mujahid, Humayd and Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read (an ra'ahu istaghna) with the hamzah shortened. The rest read ra'ahu with the hamzah lengthened, and this is the preferred reading.

Allah's saying: (Nay! Indeed, man surely transgresses) to the end of the surah. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It was also said: the whole surah was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, when the Prophet ﷺ forbade him from prayer, so Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to pray at the Masjid and to recite "in the name of your Lord." On this view, the surah is not among the first things revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that the people would not accept that, so he refrained from them out of mercy toward them. The lam has been omitted from His saying (an ra'ahu), as one says: "Indeed you transgress if you see your wealth." The Arabs omit the nafs (self) in this category: they say ra'aytani and hasibtani, and mata tarakа kharijan, and mata tazunnuka kharijan. ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ (96:8). That is, the place of return of whoever has this description, so that We will recompense him. *al-Ruj'ā* (الرُّجْعَى), *al-marji'* (الْمَرْجِعُ) and *al-ruj'ū'* (الرُّجُوعُ) are *maṣādir* (verbal nouns). It is said: *rajaʿa ilayhi rujūʿan wa marjiʿan* (رَجَعَ إِلَيْهِ رُجُوعًا وَمَرْجِعًا). And *ruj'ā* (رُجْعَى) is on the pattern *fuʿlā* (فُعْلَى).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾. It refers to Abu Jahl (ʿabdan), and it [the one who prays] is Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu Jahl said: "If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely step on his neck." This was related by Abu Hurayrah. So God sent down these verses as an expression of wonder [[That is, causing the addressee to be amazed and moving him toward wonder (from the Hashiyat al-Jamal).]] at him. It is also said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: "Is this one who forbids prayer safe from punishment?"

﴿Have you considered: if he were upon guidance, or enjoined righteousness﴾ (11–12).

That is, "Have you considered, O Abu Jahl, if Muhammad were upon this description, is not the one who forbids him from righteousness and prayer doomed?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 96, verse 13–14:

He means Abu Jahl, who denied the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, and turned away from faith. Al-Farra' (a grammarian of Kufa) said: the meaning is, "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays, while he is upon guidance and enjoins piety, and the forbidder is one who denies and turns away from the Remembrance?" That is, "How strange this is!" Then he says: "Woe to him! Did Abu Jahl not know that Allah sees?" That is, He sees him and knows his deed; so this is a confirmation and a rebuke. It was also said: each of the two "a-ra'ayta" is a substitute for the first. And "a-lam ya'lam bi-anna Allaha yara" is the predicate.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 96, verse 13–14:

He means Abu Jahl, who denied the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, and turned away from faith. Al-Farra' (a grammarian of Kufa) said: the meaning is, "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays, while he is upon guidance and enjoins piety, and the forbidder is one who denies and turns away from the Remembrance?" That is, "How strange this is!" Then he says: "Woe to him! Did Abu Jahl not know that Allah sees?" That is, He sees him and knows his deed; so this is a confirmation and a rebuke. It was also said: each of the two "a-ra'ayta" is a substitute for the first. And "a-lam ya'lam bi-anna Allaha yara" is the predicate.

**Allah's statement: ﴿Nay, if he does not desist﴾**, meaning Abu Jahl does not desist from harming you, O Muhammad. **﴿We will surely seize﴾**, meaning we will surely take hold of him by the forelock and humiliate him. It has also been said: we will take hold of him by his forelock on the Day of Resurrection, his forelock and his feet will be bound together, and he will be cast into the Fire, as Allah says: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [[Qur'an 55:41.]]. So although the verse concerns Abu Jahl, it is a warning to people and a threat to whoever refuses to obey or prevents others from obedience.

The lexicographers say: *safa'tu bil-shay'* (I seized the thing) means that I gripped it and pulled it with great force. It is also said: *safa'a bi-nasiyat farasihi* (he seized the forelock of his horse). A poet said:

*A people who, when the cries increase, you see them*
*Between one who bridles his colt and one who seizes (by the forelock).* [[The verse is by Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali, a Companion. It is also narrated as: "between one who bridles..."]]

It has also been said that the word is derived from *saf'atuhu al-nar wa al-shams*, meaning when fire and the sun change a person's face to a blackened state, as the poet said:

*Blackened hearth-stones in the place of the cooking pot,*
*And a trench like the base of a basin, broken and humbled.* [[This verse is recorded this way in all copies of the original and in Tafsir Ibn 'Adil, but it is a combination of two odes. The first half is from the Mu'allaqa (suspended ode) of Zuhayr. The verse in his Diwan and ode reads:*
*"Athafi sufa'an fi ma'arrasi mirjal / wa nuwan ka-jidhm al-hawd lam yatathalam."*
*The second half is from an ode by al-Nabigha. The verse in his Diwan reads:*
*"Ramad ka-kuhl al-'ayn la ayya abinuhu / wa nuwan ka-jidhm al-hawd athlam."*
*Khashi' (humbled) means lying flat on the ground. Al-athlam means the broken one. Al-athafi are the stones on which the cooking pot is set, one of which is called uthfiyya. Al-sufa' means black. Al-ma'arras is the place where the cooking pot is. Al-mirjal is any pot used for cooking, whether made of stone, iron, pottery or copper. Al-nuwa is a barrier of earth raised around a tent so that water does not enter from outside. Jidhm al-hawd is its edge and base. "Lam yatathalam" means the top of the nuwa has gone, but what remains has not broken, i.e., has not been crushed.]]

**Al-nasiya** is the hair of the front of the head. It may be used to refer to the whole person, as one says, "this is a blessed forelock," meaning the whole person. Allah specified the forelock by mention, following the Arab custom: when they wished to humiliate and disgrace someone, they seized his forelock.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-saf'* is pulling with force, meaning "we will drag him by his forelock into the Fire." It has also been said that *al-saf'* is striking, meaning "we will slap his face." All of these meanings are close, namely that he will be struck when seized and then dragged into Hell.

Then Allah said, as an apposition (*badal*, a grammatical substitution of a noun for the one before it): ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾, meaning the forelock of Abu Jahl is lying in what it says and sinful in what it does. The one who is sinful (*khati'*) is one who is held to account and seized, whereas the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is not seized. [[Al-khati': one who intentionally does what is not fitting, i.e., one who aims at sin. Al-mukhti': one who intended what is right but arrived at something else.]]

Describing the forelock as lying and sinful is like describing faces as looking, in Allah's statement: ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ [[Qur'an 75:23.]]. It has also been said that the meaning is: its owner is a liar and a sinner, as one says, "his day is fasting and his night is standing," meaning he fasts during his day and stands in prayer during his night.

**Allah's statement: ﴿Nay, if he does not desist﴾**, meaning Abu Jahl does not desist from harming you, O Muhammad. **﴿We will surely seize﴾**, meaning we will surely take hold of him by the forelock and humiliate him. It has also been said: we will take hold of him by his forelock on the Day of Resurrection, his forelock and his feet will be bound together, and he will be cast into the Fire, as Allah says: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [[Qur'an 55:41.]]. So although the verse concerns Abu Jahl, it is a warning to people and a threat to whoever refuses to obey or prevents others from obedience.

The lexicographers say: *safa'tu bil-shay'* (I seized the thing) means that I gripped it and pulled it with great force. It is also said: *safa'a bi-nasiyat farasihi* (he seized the forelock of his horse). A poet said:

*A people who, when the cries increase, you see them*
*Between one who bridles his colt and one who seizes (by the forelock).* [[The verse is by Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali, a Companion. It is also narrated as: "between one who bridles..."]]

It has also been said that the word is derived from *saf'atuhu al-nar wa al-shams*, meaning when fire and the sun change a person's face to a blackened state, as the poet said:

*Blackened hearth-stones in the place of the cooking pot,*
*And a trench like the base of a basin, broken and humbled.* [[This verse is recorded this way in all copies of the original and in Tafsir Ibn 'Adil, but it is a combination of two odes. The first half is from the Mu'allaqa (suspended ode) of Zuhayr. The verse in his Diwan and ode reads:*
*"Athafi sufa'an fi ma'arrasi mirjal / wa nuwan ka-jidhm al-hawd lam yatathalam."*
*The second half is from an ode by al-Nabigha. The verse in his Diwan reads:*
*"Ramad ka-kuhl al-'ayn la ayya abinuhu / wa nuwan ka-jidhm al-hawd athlam."*
*Khashi' (humbled) means lying flat on the ground. Al-athlam means the broken one. Al-athafi are the stones on which the cooking pot is set, one of which is called uthfiyya. Al-sufa' means black. Al-ma'arras is the place where the cooking pot is. Al-mirjal is any pot used for cooking, whether made of stone, iron, pottery or copper. Al-nuwa is a barrier of earth raised around a tent so that water does not enter from outside. Jidhm al-hawd is its edge and base. "Lam yatathalam" means the top of the nuwa has gone, but what remains has not broken, i.e., has not been crushed.]]

**Al-nasiya** is the hair of the front of the head. It may be used to refer to the whole person, as one says, "this is a blessed forelock," meaning the whole person. Allah specified the forelock by mention, following the Arab custom: when they wished to humiliate and disgrace someone, they seized his forelock.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-saf'* is pulling with force, meaning "we will drag him by his forelock into the Fire." It has also been said that *al-saf'* is striking, meaning "we will slap his face." All of these meanings are close, namely that he will be struck when seized and then dragged into Hell.

Then Allah said, as an apposition (*badal*, a grammatical substitution of a noun for the one before it): ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾, meaning the forelock of Abu Jahl is lying in what it says and sinful in what it does. The one who is sinful (*khati'*) is one who is held to account and seized, whereas the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is not seized. [[Al-khati': one who intentionally does what is not fitting, i.e., one who aims at sin. Al-mukhti': one who intended what is right but arrived at something else.]]

Describing the forelock as lying and sinful is like describing faces as looking, in Allah's statement: ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ [[Qur'an 75:23.]]. It has also been said that the meaning is: its owner is a liar and a sinner, as one says, "his day is fasting and his night is standing," meaning he fasts during his day and stands in prayer during his night.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 96, verses 17–18:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾, meaning the people of his council and his tribe, so let him seek help from them.

(﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾), that is, the angels, who are harsh and severe. This is related from Ibn Abbas and others. Their singular is *zibniyy*, as said by al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash said: *za'bin*. Abu Ubayda said: *zibniyah*. It is also said: *zabaniyy*. It is also said that it is a collective noun, like *al-ababil* and *al-aba'id*. Qatadah said: they are the police (*shurat*) in the speech of the Arabs. The word is derived from *al-zabn*, which means repelling, and from it comes *al-muzabanah* (a sale of fresh dates on the palm trees in exchange for dried dates, which the Prophet forbade because of the deception and uncertainty it contains) in trade. It is also said that they were called *al-zabaniyah* because they work with their feet just as they work with their hands. This was related by Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: It is reported in a report that when the Prophet ﷺ recited this surah and reached His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will seize him by the forelock﴾, Abu Jahl said: "I will call my people so that they will prevent your Lord from [harming] me." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell.﴾ When he heard mention of the guards of Hell, he returned in fright. It was said to him: "Did you fear him?" He said: "No! But I saw beside him a horseman threatening me with the guards." I do not know what the *zabaniyah* are, and the horseman inclined toward me, so I feared that he would devour me.

It is also reported in reports that the guards' heads are in the sky and their feet are on the earth, and they push the disbelievers into Hell. It is also said that they are the greatest of the angels in creation and the strongest in seizing. The Arabs use this name for one whose seizing is severe. The poet said:

*Feeders in the drought, spearmen in the battle,*
*guards, stout-necked, great in their wisdom.*

[Ghulb: plural of aghlab, meaning thick-necked. The Arabs describe chiefs by thickness and length of the neck. Al-hulum: plural of hilm, meaning intellect.]

And from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾, he said: Abu Jahl said: "If I see Muhammad praying, I will certainly step on his neck." The Prophet ﷺ said: "[If he had done so, the angels would have seized him openly.]" Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hadith that is *hasan sahih gharib*. Ikrimah also related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Abu Jahl passed by the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying near the Maqam, and said: "Did I not forbid you from this, O Muhammad!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke harshly to him, and Abu Jahl said: "With what will you threaten me, O Muhammad! By Allah, I am the one with the greatest assembly in this valley." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "By Allah, if he had called his assembly, the guards of the punishment would have seized him at that very moment." Al-Tirmidhi related it with a similar meaning and said: *hasan gharib sahih*.

In the speech of the Arabs, *al-nadi* is the gathering place where people meet (*yantadi*), that is, they assemble, and what is meant is the people of the assembly, as Jarir said:

*They have a gathering, red-bearded, humbled,*
*equal, its free men and its slaves alike.*

[The rest of the verse: "equal, its free men and its slaves alike." The line is actually by Dhu al-Rummah, not Jarir. Suhb: red. Al-sibal: the hair on the right and left of the upper lip.]

And Zuhayr said:

*Among them are the stations, their faces are handsome,*
*and gatherings frequented by speech and deed.*

[The stations: the councils. They were called "stations" because a man would stand in the council and urge toward good and reconcile people. Andiyah: plural of nadan, which also means council, and this is the evidence in the line.]

And another said:

*And after you, O Kulayb, the council has been plundered.*

[This is the second half of a line by al-Muhalhil lamenting his brother Kulayb. Its first half:
"I was told that the fire was kindled after you."]

I called (*nadaytu*) the man, I call him (*unadihi*), when I sat with him. Zuhayr said:

*The neighbor of the House and the man who calls (al-munadi)*
*before the tribe, their pact is the same.*

(Kallā) That is, the matter is not as Abu Jahl supposes.

(Lā tuṭiʿhu) That is, in what he calls you to of abandoning the prayer.

(Wa-sjud) That is, pray to God. (Wa-qtarib) That is, draw near to God, exalted is His praise, through obedience and worship. It has also been said: the meaning is: when you prostrate, draw near to God through supplication.

ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord, and the most beloved to Him, is when his forehead is on the ground prostrating to God." Our scholars said: That is because prostration is the utmost of servitude and humility, while to God belongs the utmost of might, and to Him belongs a might without measure. So the further you are from His attributes, the nearer you are to His Paradise, and the closer you come to His neighborhood in His abode. In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for bowing, glorify the Lord in it; as for prostration, strive in supplication, for it is qamin (fitting and deserving) that your supplication be answered." (It is said: qamin and qamin, with the mim vowelled with a fatḥah or a kasrah; the one with the kasrah is dualised and pluralised, like qamin, meaning fitting and deserving.)

And how well the one who said:

"When the necks humble themselves in lowliness
toward You from us, their might lies in their humility."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: Prostrate, you, O Muhammad, praying; and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: "Wa-sjud" is from prostration. It may mean prostration in prayer, and it may mean the prostration of recitation in this surah. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The apparent meaning is the prostration of prayer," due to His saying, exalted is He: "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays... to His saying... Nay, do not obey him, and prostrate and draw near," were it not for what is established in the Sahih in the narration of Muslim and other imams from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "I prostrated with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in (Idhā as-samāʾu nshaqqat) [al-Inshiqaq: 1], and in (Iqra bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq) [al-ʿAlaq: 1], two prostrations." So this was an explicit statement that the intended meaning is the prostration of recitation.

Ibn Wahb narrated from Hammad ibn Zayd, from ʿAsim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The obligatory prostrations are four: Alif Lam Mim (al-Sajdah), Ha Mim (Tanzil min al-Rahman al-Rahim), al-Najm, and Iqra bi-smi rabbika."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: If this is authentic, it entails a second prostration in Surah al-Hajj as well, even though it is coupled with bowing, because its meaning would be: bow in the place of bowing, and prostrate in the place of prostration.

Ibn Nafiʿ and Mutarrif said: Malik used to prostrate privately at the end of this surah, (Iqra bi-smi rabbika), while Ibn Wahb regarded it as one of the obligatory prostrations. I say: We have also transmitted, from the hadith of Malik ibn Anas, from Rabiʿah ibn Abi ʿAbd al-Rahman, from Nafiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: When God, exalted is He, revealed (Iqra bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq) [al-ʿAlaq: 1], the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Muʿadh: "Write it down, O Muʿadh." Muʿadh took the tablet, the pen, and the nun, which is the inkwell, and wrote it. When he reached (Nay, do not obey him, and prostrate and draw near), the tablet prostrated, the pen prostrated, and the nun prostrated, and they were saying: "O God, raise through it a remembrance, O God, lower through it a burden, O God, forgive through it a sin." Muʿadh said: I prostrated, and informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he prostrated. The surah is concluded. All praise is due to God for what He has opened, bestowed and given. To Him belong praise and favour.
